Optimizing additively manufactured mouthguards: An evaluation of multi-layer materials for improved shock absorption and durability compared to conventionally fabricated samples

Chenyuan Li1, Takahiro Wada2, Yumi Tsuchida3, Kairi Hayashi1, Gen Tanabe1,4, Toshiaki Ueno1,4, and Hiroshi Churei1*

1Department of Masticatory Function and Health Science, Graduate School of Medical and Dental Science, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Tokyo, Japan

2Department of Advanced Biomaterials, Graduate School of Medical and Dental Science, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Tokyo, Japan

3Department of Digital Dentistry, Graduate School of Medical and Dental Science, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Tokyo, Japan

4Department of Sports Dentistry, School of Dentistry, Meikai University, Sakado, Japan

## Abstract

Although sports mouthguards (MGs) are mandatory in some contact sports, the use of conventional fabricated materials for making MGs is time-consuming and lacks precision, limiting their widespread application. In this study, we compared mouthguards designed using digital software with conventional ones. The conventional mouthguards were categorized into two types: those constructed from a poly-(ethylene vinyl acetate)-base material, and those constructed from MG21, a polyolefin-base material. The shock absorption and durability were assessed through a free-falling steel ball test and a fatigue test. The durability of the MGs was evaluated by measuring the retention force in the inner layer and deviations at consistent points on the outer layer during various fatigue test stages. Additively manufactured samples showed superior shock absorption performance, except for the double-layer samples with an inner layer of Shore A hardness 95. All single-layer additively manufactured MGs were damaged during the mid-fatigue test stage, while both double-layer additively manufactured and conventional MGs remained undamaged. Throughout all fatigue test stages, the retention force of double-layer additively manufactured MGs was significantly lower than that of conventional MGs. However, the retention force of double-layer additively manufactured samples with an inner layer of Shore A hardness 70 (D-A70) was superior to the average of all MGs in the wet condition, which was 6.4 ± 2.5 N in the previous study. The results of this study demonstrated the benefits of a hybrid design of hard and soft materials, particularly the promising combination of D-A70, which exhibited comparable shock absorption and durability to conventional MGs.

Keywords: Sports mouthguards; Additively manufactured; Photoinitiator; Shock absorption; Durability; Retention force

## 1. Introduction

A sports mouthguard (MG) is essential for protecting the hard and soft tissues of the oral cavity, including teeth and gums, from impact during athletic activities. The World Dental Federation emphasizes the importance of custommade sports MGs in preventing trauma.1 In certain contact sports, such as boxing, MGs usage is mandatory because they reduce the risk of traumatic dental injuries and brain concussions, as demonstrated by extensive research.2-8

Despite their importance, creating a comfortable and durable MG is a complex challenge. The fabrication process, particularly the thermoforming phase, often results in diminished thickness around the anterior teeth, which can affect both comfort and protection.9 Additionally, each MG must be tailored to fit comfortably, adding to the complexity of the design.

The emergence of three-dimensional (3D) digital design and additive manufacturing process, known for its customization, rapid production, and cost-efficiency, has attracted substantial interest. Prior studies have validated its safety and effectiveness,10-13 suggesting a promising future for additively manufactured sports MGs.

In 2020, Li et al. published an extensive exposition of the digital design and manufacturing of sports MGs.14

By implementing a semi-digital workflow, Hada et al. examined how temperature fluctuations affected the material properties of sports MGs.15 After investigating various materials, Sousa et al.16 found that three additively manufactured materials—recycled polylactic acid (rPLA), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), and high-impact polystyrene (HIPS)—outperformed a conventional material, poly-(ethylene vinyl acetate) (EVA) in the shock absorption experiment. A study by Pinho et al.17 demonstrated increased elasticity and resistance in aged sandwich samples.

The processes are categorized into International Organization for Standardization/American Society for Testing and Materials (ISO/ASTM) process classes in medical applications of additively manufactured powder bed fusion, material extrusion, vat photopolymerization, material jetting, binder jetting, sheet lamination, and directed energy deposition.18 The Polyjet process (Stratasys Ltd., Rehovot, Israel), a revolutionary multi-material jetting process, was widely applied for higher precision and printing speed, the ability to print multiple materials, and hands-free removal of support structure.19

Materials of acrylate-base photoinitiator composites (Agilus, Vero, digital poly-(acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene) [D-ABS]) are preferred for additively manufactured MGs due to their excellent protection capability, which is the

most critical ability of MG. These materials are competitive with those of conventional fabricated materials like EVA and polyolefin (PO).20,21 It has been demonstrated that incorporating a hard insert within a conventional material can significantly enhance the protection capability.22

While the shock absorption and dispersion properties of additively manufactured MGs have been extensively studied, there is a need for more focused research on their durability, especially considering the intermittent occlusal forces during athletic activities.21 Durability is another crucial factor for the long-term, effective, and safe use of MGs. The resistance to surface wear and deformation from continuous use has been evaluated for conventional MG materials,23 but the durability of additively manufactured MGs requires further investigation. Hard occlusal surfaces in devices such as night guards, which prevent bruxism, have been shown to improve durability and reduce wear.24

This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of combining hard and soft materials in additively manufactured MGs to enhance shock absorption and dispersion properties in simulated oral environments. Additionally, it evaluated the durability, retention force, and morphological changes of these MGs, particularly in response to the effects of intermittent occlusal forces on their surfaces in simulated oral environments.

## 2. Materials and methods

2.1. Samples preparation and digital model design Acrylate-base photoinitiator composites Agilus, Vero, and D-ABS (Stratasys Ltd., Rehovot, Israel) were utilized (Table 1). Seven types of Agilus and/or Vero composites with Shore A hardness values of 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 85, and 95 were produced under controlled conditions of 20±5℃ and 50% humidity, denoted as A30, A40, A50, A60, A70, A85, and A95, respectively (Table 2). The composites were blended in their liquid state before the printing process.25 Single-layer samples were specified as having a diameter of 50 mm and a thickness of 3 mm. Double-layer samples consist of a 0.5 mm thick hard layer of D-ABS and a 2.5 mm thick, soft layer of Agilus or/and Vero composites (A30- 95), designated as D-A30 through D-A95, respectively (Figure 1). Material samples were printed by a J850 Digital Anatomy 3D printer (Stratasys Ltd., Rehovot, Israel) with a dual-head liquid output. Conventional MG sheets made of PO-base material (MG21; CGK, Hiroshima, Japan) and EVA-base material (Erkoflex [ERK]; Erkodent Erich Kopp GmbH, Pfalzgrafenweiler, Germany) were molded for comparison. The shock absorption test was conducted on 16 samples.

2.2. Shock absorption test According to Fukusawa et al.’s research,26 a shock absorption test was conducted using a 32.6 g metal ball with a 20 mm diameter, dropped from a height of about 615 mm onto a steel platform. A load cell sensor system was positioned at the bottom of the impact load machine. In this research, physical experiments were performed in a simulated oral environment to be consistent with future clinical evaluations.27 Samples were placed in a thermostat set at 37°C and 100% relative humidity for 24 h before testing. A custom-made chamber maintained the sample temperature and humidity during the shock absorption test.

A previous study showed that the fracture load of human teeth falls within the range of 689–1093 N.28 In the same mechanical situation, to verify the protective effect of MG, the impact force without a sample in this experiment was controlled within this range. Impact loads were measured using three dynamic compression load cells

(LMA-A-1kN; Kyowa Electronic Instruments Co., Tokyo, Japan) with a capacity of 1 kilo Newton (kN), arranged in a triangle under a 10 mm thick stainless-steel platform. The sample was centered on this platform. During the test, loads were recorded at a 50 kHz sampling rate using data analysis software (EDX-100A and DCS-100A, Kyowa Electronic Instruments, Inc.). The total impact load was the sum of the three load cell readings, with the maximum load defined as the maximal impact force (MIF). The arrival time to MIF was denoted as MIF-t. Each sample was tested five times (Figure 3).26

2.3. Fatigue test The fatigue test was designed on the basis of Sugimoto et al.’s research.29 A concavity was ground at the center of gravity on the maxillary stone model plane. An iron ball was placed in this concavity on the maxillary stone model, which was worn with a MG and meshed with the mandibular stone model. Loading forces were examined

Retention force evaluation of MG inlayer in fatigue test According to Karaganeva et al.’s study,30 a parallel plate and three hooks were molded from personal tray material (Ostron II, GC Corporation, Tokyo, Japan). A parallel plate was attached to the universal testing machine, and three hooks were utilized to pull the MG sample from the upper dental stone model.

A retention force test was executed on each MG by hooking the labial or buccal and palatal margins of three anatomical points including anterior and posterior (center

A retention force test was conducted on each MG by hooking the labial or buccal and palatal margins at three anatomical locations. Shock absorption and fatigue tests were conducted under the same setup conditions for temperature and humidity control (Figure 5).

Each MG was hauled from the maxillary model at a constant rate of 50 mm/min.30 The test was executed five times on a universal machine (SCG-5KNA, Shimadzu Corporation), with data output from the software (Trapezium x, version 1.4.0, Shimadzu Corporation). The gauges were recalibrated after each measurement. The maximum force represented the retention force. The retention forces of conventionally fabricated and additively manufactured MGs were recorded in pre- (0th), mid- (5000th), and post- (10,000th) fatigue tests.

## 3. Results

3.1. MIF and MIF-t during shock absorption test The MIF of the free-falling steel ball without a sample was 709.0 ± 16.7 N. The MIF of conventional materials, ERK and MG21, were 386.5 ± 5.5 N and 393.9 ± 6.9 N, respectively. The MIF for single-layer additively manufactured samples increased progressively from 245.8 ± 3.2 N to 318.5 ± 10.8 N with increasing Shore A hardness of materials.

The lowest MIF among the double-layer additively manufactured samples was observed for D-A70 at 328.2 ± 7.3 N, with values increasing sequentially on both sides of the Shore A hardness scale. All additively manufactured materials (except D-A95) absorbed more impact force than conventional materials ERK and MG21 (Figure 6).

Each single-layer additively manufactured sample was statistically significant compared to its corresponding double-layer additively manufactured sample of the same hardness of soft layer that was superior to the double-layer sample in shock absorption (all pairs; P < 0.001).

3.2. Durability under cycle-loading fatigue test All single-layer additively manufactured MG samples had cracks on the molar occlusal surface by approximately the 1000th cycle. These cracks of the MG’s occlusal surface were bitten through by the 5000th cycle; all single-layer additively manufactured MG samples were discontinued during the mid-fatigue test (Figure 10). Table 3 shows the statistical significance among the three types of MG samples (conventional, n = 6; single-layer additively manufactured, n = 9; double-layer additively manufactured, n = 9) (P < 0.001). Double-layer additively manufactured MG samples and conventionally fabricated MG samples were more durable than single-layer additively manufactured MG samples.

3.2.1. Assessment of retention force in MG inlayer There was a statistical significance in retention force between each conventionally fabricated MG and each double-layer additively manufactured MG sample at any fatigue test stage (P < 0.001). In the comparison of retention forces, only MG21 had a statistical significance that increased retention force throughout the whole fatigue tests (P = 0.028); significant increases in retention force were also observed from the pre- to post-fatigue test (P = 0.043). In general, all MGs showed an inapparent increase in retention force from the pre-fatigue test to the mid-fatigue test (Table 4). During the fatigue test, the retention force in double-layer additively manufactured MG samples was found to be increased corresponding to the higher value in Shore A hardness of soft-layer materials (A) (Figure 11).

3.2.2. Assessment of morphological changes in MG outer layer MG outer layer morphological changes were evaluated using RMS values. There was no statistical significance in RMS values in the pre-mid and mid-post fatigue test periods for MG samples (conventional, n = 6; double-layer additively manufactured, n = 9) (P = 0.159 and P = 0.438, respectively) (Table 5). Compared to pre-mid and pre-post fatigue tests, the RMS of ERK samples decreased after a period of cycle-loading fatigue tests. ## 4. Discussion

Most existing articles mainly focus on the digital design and 3D printing processes of additively manufactured sports MGs or the physical performance testing of these materials. So far, sports MGs have mainly been examined for their shock absorption property; in additively manufactured MGs, durability is insufficient compared to conventionally

manufactured MGs. Thus, this study examines the possibility of improving shock-absorbing ability and durability. been validated. Moreover, the clinical perspective was not considered. Schewe et al. explored the shock absorption of photoinitiators, but did not clarify the specific requirements for designing MGs with a thickness of 2–4 mm.37 MGs thicker than 4 mm may cause joint discomfort due to the 2–4 mm freeway space in the mouth.38 Previous studies have not extensively considered the effects of the oral environment, such as temperature and humidity.21,37 Most experiments have been executed at room temperature and humidity because the conditions follow international standards, and are globally applicable.39 In Tun et al.’s study,21 the shock absorption rate of Agilus30 at room temperature was 26.9%, but it increased to 65.3% in this study. As with Compo50, Agilus50 (A50) showed an increased absorption rate from 44.8% at room temperature and humidity to 63.3% under simulated oral conditions. In contrast, conventional MG materials, ERK and MG21, demonstrated consistent absorption rates of around 43.5% and 41.8% at room temperature, and approximately 45.5% and 44.5% under simulated oral conditions. Our study demonstrated that additively manufactured material samples had an improvement in shock absorption in a simulated oral environment.

Both layer design and Shore A hardness affect shock absorption properties. The free-falling steel ball test indicated layered design was more influential than hardness of materials, as demonstrated by statistical significance between hardness-paired material samples (Figure 7). The MIF-t approximation function for single-layer samples suggested a more complex relationship, with an additional peak in growth after A70 samples, encouraging further investigation (Figure 9).

Our research confirmed that double-layer additively manufactured MG samples were preferred to single-layer MG samples, as the single-layer MG samples can be damaged at fatigue tests. Despite the superior shock absorption ability of single-layer additively manufactured samples, their propensity to crack during cycle-loading fatigue tests suggests that single-layer designs are not feasible for future use. Double-layer additively manufactured MG samples exhibited superior shock absorption than conventionally fabricated MG samples ERK and MG21, except for the type of D-A95 samples. In addition, double-layer additively manufactured materials (D-A50, D-A60, D-A70) had the same MIF-t values as conventional materials.

Our research also proved that fabricating inconsistencies affected the retention force of conventionally fabricated MG samples. However, additively manufactured MG samples have manufacturing consistencies, superior shock absorption, and acceptable durability, providing more consistent, standardized, and reliable safety protection.

In addition to shock absorption, a MG must ensure a sufficient retention force to avoid dislocation during rapid movement. Previous research30 indicated that the average retention force of conventionally fabricated MGs was 6.4 ± 2.5 N in wet conditions. This value was exceeded only by D-A70 type of MG samples when without any use. The MG sample is expected to have more specialized applications for individuals involved in fast-moving contact sports, such as football players and boxers.

According to the evaluation of retention force and RMS, only MG21 samples showed a statistical significance of a larger retention force with a smaller RMS deviation in fatigue tests (Tables 5 and 6). However, previous studies suggest that the MG retention force decreases with continued use.40 MGs initially increase or stand the retention force before decreasing it. This may be conducive to the preparation of MG samples in future clinical applications. Further research is necessary to determine the most appropriate load preparation for MGs during fatigue tests.

There are some limitations in our study. We excluded certain values due to similar shock absorption results between the intermediate Shore A hardness number of additively manufactured material samples. Besides, the unsatisfactory results of the shock absorption tests conducted in MIF-t on D-A85 and D-A95 types of material samples removed the need for further durability tests, potentially resulting in a data exclusion. Biocompatibility is another consideration. Agilus series materials have already been applied in several medical devices, including stethoscopes41 and eye gear with prescription glasses,42 and the same type of materials are being employed in this study. However, little is known about the biocompatibility of these materials. Despite these limitations, the findings of this study may contribute to MG enhancement as a medical device in the future.

## 5. Conclusion

In this study, additively manufactured material samples (except for D-A95) made by Agilus, Vero, and D-ABS performed better in shock absorption than conventional material samples ERK and MG21 in simulated oral environments, with additively manufactured single-layer MG samples and specific types of double-layer MG samples (D-A50, D-A60, D-A70) demonstrating the same arrival time of maximum impact force (MIF-t) as conventionally fabricated MGs.

Moreover, this study provides insights into the durability and retention forces of additively manufactured MG samples, indicating that single-layer additively manufactured MG samples are less durable, but highlighting the benefits of utilizing hard materials on occlusal surfaces and effective shock absorption capabilities
